43bf4eeed6.why: Both judge issues are fixed: the dead lure 'a still ball keeps its momentum stored' is replaced by the real misconception that momentum is kept only in bouncy collisions (false: the law needs only no net outside force), and the key no longer repeats 'cloth'. Key true; the three lures are each false (heat takes energy, not momentum; the law is not limited to bouncy collisions; it holds only with no outside force). Exactly one defensible answer. A grade deeper than the T2 cue-ball energy question, not a re-ask; no other final asks the outside-force condition. Voice clean ('their' = the balls).

17b2a36a11.why: The T4 tackle re-ask is gone: the stem now asks the size of her momentum against his, the conservation fact (equal and opposite, total zero), not who accelerates or glides faster, and the T2 third-law lure is dropped. Key true; 'twice as big' (speed only) and 'half as big' (mass only) are the real half-counts. Minor: 'Zero, like his' is the weakest lure, since the stem has both gliding, but it is the total-for-each confusion and the judge proposed it, so it stays live enough. 'In opposite directions' is out of the stem, so nothing echoes the key. Not the T2 rope-skaters fact (third law). Voice clean.

7d9a044f3c.why: The fact-check error is fixed: the card no longer makes Huygens the finder of the soft-body failure or of heat ('as was learned much later', Joule, 1840s). Huygens's collision rules were for elastic (hard) bodies, and the stem now says so ('worked out for hard bodies, that is kept in these lumps too'). The partly true 'heat' lure is replaced by 'the time each collision lasts', which is in no conserved count. Key (direction) confirmed: Huygens kept the quantity of motion toward one side, a vector. 'Square of each body's speed' is truly wrong for clay that stops dead. Overlap with ba63ed1a27 softened as the judge asked. Descartes 1644 and his scalar count confirmed.

a979ea77bb.why: The card no longer says a steady speed pressed on no one on this run. It now says the wind beat on him at top speed (no windshield) but far less than the stop, as NASA's history puts it: windblast 'negligible and unnoticeable in comparison with deceleration effects'. Key true (the same speed change in 1.4 s against 5 s). Every lure is still wrong. Stapp, Sonic Wind No. 1, New Mexico, December 1954, 632 mph, 5 s, 1.4 s and 18 g in the textbooks of the day all confirmed. 46.2 g is the commonly cited peak; NASA's own peaks are 35-40 g, and either is more than twice 18. Not a T4 re-ask.

28269a7320.why: The lure that 'built to crumple' killed ('springs back') is replaced by the impact-speed misconception, truly wrong: crumpling starts only once the car has hit, and the momentum to lose is set by mass and impact speed. All four choices are now live. Key true (longer stop, smaller average force). Barenyi at Daimler-Benz, the rigid-car view he questioned, patent 854157 granted 1952, and the 1959 W111 as the first carbody built to it all confirmed. Distinct from the T3 unbuckled passenger and from e0e900c697's fact.

e0e900c697.why: The elimination tell is gone. The question asks only the change in momentum, and it has three live misconceptions against the key: the knees soak some up; a slower stop means a smaller change; a longer push means a larger change. The last is false: the ground's own push does grow with a longer stop, but her momentum change (rest from the same landing speed) does not. Key true: the same wall top gives the same landing speed. 'From the same height' is out of the stem, so nothing echoes 'the same'. No other final asks landing or knees; the impulse invariant here is distinct from a979ea77bb and 28269a7320.
